Home Business News Banking and Finance Capital Market and Commodity Exchange Construction, Steel and Cement Energy and Mining ICT and Telecom Import and Export Latest Business Alerts Manufacturing Transport and Logistics Startups Tenders Business Directory Doing Business Starting A Business General Info Industry Finance Mining Communication Import and Export Regulations Procedures Payment Methods Shipping Regulations Procedures Shipping Info Customs Regulations Procedures Tariff and Duty HS Code Labour Investment Regulations Procedures Incentives Opportunities Options Tax Types Appeal Regulations Procedures Construction Home » Business News » Banking and Finance » Mastercard Introduces AI and Tokenization to Enhance Digital Payment Security in Ethiopia Mastercard Introduces AI and Tokenization to Enhance Digital Payment Security in Ethiopia Details Category: Banking and Finance View Comments Mastercard is strengthening digital payment security in Ethiopia by deploying artificial intelligence and tokenization technology as electronic transactions become increasingly common. The move comes amid growing use of mobile wallets, virtual cards and contactless payments, alongside concerns about cybercrime and financial fraud. According to the National Bank of Ethiopia, fraud losses totaled Birr 1.3 billion in 2024. Attempted cyberattacks against public and private institutions also rose by 115 percent during the first half of 2024 compared with the corresponding period in 2023. Mastercard's AI-powered systems can assess transaction risks within milliseconds, helping identify suspicious activity while reducing unnecessary declines of legitimate payments. In March 2026, the company introduced a transaction specific AI foundation model trained on hundreds of millions of anonymized transactions. The technology is designed to recognize complex fraud patterns that conventional detection systems may miss. The company is also promoting tokenization, which replaces actual card numbers with secure digital identifiers during transactions. By limiting exposure of sensitive payment information, the technology helps protect customers using online stores, digital wallets and contactless terminals. These measures complement Ethiopia's efforts to modernize its financial infrastructure, improve payment interoperability and reduce dependence on cash. Mastercard's local partnerships include initiatives with Dashen Bank and Ethiopian Airlines, such as the ShebaMiles Premium Cards, which offer travel benefits and international payment functionality. ethiopia.summary: Mastercard has announced the introduction of advanced AI and tokenization technologies to bolster digital payment security in Ethiopia. This initiative aims to enhance the safety and efficiency of online transactions, addressing the growing concerns over digital fraud and cyber threats. By implementing tokenization, Mastercard will replace sensitive payment information with unique identification symbols, ensuring that actual card details are not exposed during transactions. This move is part of Mastercard's broader strategy to support the digital economy in Ethiopia, which is experiencing rapid growth in e-commerce and mobile payments. The company emphasizes that these innovations will not only protect consumers but also foster trust in digital payment systems, encouraging more users to engage in online financial activities. Mastercard's efforts align with the Ethiopian government's goals to promote financial inclusion and digital transformation across the country.

ethiopia.title: Drought, Food Shortages and Child Malnutrition Deepen Humanitarian Needs in Afar, Amhara and Tigray
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Drought, Food Shortages and Child Malnutrition Deepen Humanitarian Needs in Afar, Amhara and Tigray - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Drought, Food Shortages and Child Malnutrition Deepen Humanitarian Needs in Afar, Amhara and Tigray World Food Programme South Omo zone in Ethiopia is facing a severe drought (file photo) 27 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Drought, rising food prices, shortages of essential medicines and disruptions to health services are compounding humanitarian needs across northern Ethiopia's Afar , Amhara and Tigray regions , with displaced children particularly vulnerable to acute malnutrition, according to a humanitarian assessment document seen by Addis Standard. The assessment, dated October 19 and covering developments between October 12 and 19, warns that the humanitarian consequences of escalating insecurity are unfolding against a backdrop of unmet needs left by the 2020-2022 northern Ethiopia conflict, subsequent episodes of fighting and displacement, and El Niño-related drought. "Needs are likely to remain high," the assessment states, noting that the combined pressures have compounded existing humanitarian vulnerabilities across Tigray, Amhara and Afar. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn One of the clearest indicators of the crisis is the nutritional situation among displaced children in Tigray. Screening conducted in September and October in Laelay Adiabo, Axum and Adwa found that approximately 15% of around 11,800 children screened in internally displaced communities had moderate acute malnutrition. The assessment cautions that information on the overall scale and severity of humanitarian needs remains fragmented. "At the time of writing, there is no needs assessment data available," it states, identifying rapid humanitarian needs assessments as a priority as access improves. Food insecurity is being aggravated by crop failures, dwindling household resources and rising prices. In Raya Azebo woreda in southern Tigray, drought has devastated agricultural production, leaving households struggling to afford basic food. More than 15,000 of the woreda's 26,000 hectares of farmland had reportedly been cultivated, but only around 400 hectares showed crop growth, according to the assessment. Approximately 10,000 hectares were not planted because of a lack of rainfall in May. A farmer quoted in the assessment said households could no longer afford basic food as prices soared while agricultural production collapsed. Many had exhausted their savings after almost a year without a meaningful harvest. Livestock owners have also suffered as animal prices fell, buyers became scarce, and livestock died from a lack of fodder and disease. Earlier this month, FEWS NET projected Crisis-level food insecurity outcomes, classified as IPC Phase 3 , will persist until January 2027 in parts of southern and eastern Tigray and lowland areas along the Tekeze River catchment. Health services under pressure The crisis is also straining an already fragile healthcare system. Hospitals in Sheraro are reportedly struggling to maintain services amid insecurity, shortages of medical supplies and prolonged delays in salary payments to civil servants. The assessment says unpaid salaries have contributed to health workers leaving the area, further reducing the availability of care. Transporting medical supplies through areas affected by fighting remains difficult, while insecurity is limiting civilians' ability to reach health facilities. Hospitals and other health facilities in Wukro and Adwa, as well as at Adigrat University, have reportedly been looted or vandalized. A cholera outbreak in Wag Hamra zone in Amhara remains a concern, with humanitarian sources reporting limited availability of treatment supplies, including fluids. Mental health needs in conflict-affected parts of Afar also remain high, the assessment notes. There have, however, been signs of improvement in humanitarian access to Tigray. An inter-agency convoy delivered essential supplies, including medicines, to northern Ethiopia on October 14, while the World Health Organization dispatched more than 71 tons of medical supplies. Hospitals in Tigray have also begun resuming operations. The resumption of humanitarian flights to Mekelle and increased movement along the Semera-Abaala-Mekelle corridor have helped humanitarian organizations move personnel and supplies into the region. The International Committee of the Red Cross and the Ethiopian Red Cross Society also delivered essential equipment and medicines to hospitals in Shire, Maichew, Mekhoni and Alamata, as well as Chercher Health Centre. Despite these developments, the assessment warns that access remains difficult or unsafe in areas experiencing active hostilities. In Amhara, road blockages and insecurity continue to delay convoy movements, while humanitarian personnel have reportedly faced harassment, theft and demands for money. Displacement and access to basic necessities Displacement across Tigray, Afar and Amhara has largely remained within the same districts or zones, according to the assessment. However, the scale of new movements remains uncertain. Civilians in rural parts of northwestern Tigray have reportedly moved toward Shire amid ongoing hostilities and heavy artillery fire. The assessment warns that new arrivals could intensify pressure on shelter and services in areas already hosting large internally displaced populations. In Afar, an estimated 11,000 to 13,000 people may remain displaced, although the figures are difficult to verify. Some people previously displaced from areas including Abaala and Megale have reportedly returned home as security and humanitarian access improved. There was a problem processing your submission. Please try again later. In eastern Tigray, restrictions on movement and blocked roads have also disrupted access to food and essential goods. In Zala Anbesa, few supplies were reportedly reaching the town as of October 15, prices were rising sharply, and shops, restaurants and other businesses had closed, affecting both livelihoods and access to basic necessities. The assessment warns that continued or intensified fighting could further undermine food security by restricting market supplies, prolonging shortages of cash and fuel, and driving up staple food prices. Education has also been disrupted. Schools in Erob, Gulo Mekeda and Zala Anbesa in eastern Tigray remain closed, while the reported use of school facilities by armed actors in Tahtay Koraro has interrupted classes during the school year. The full extent of the humanitarian crisis remains difficult to establish because of limited access, incomplete information and disrupted administrative structures. In Tigray, interruptions to the regional agriculture and disaster risk management institutions have also weakened local capacity to respond to drought. The assessment concludes that improving humanitarian access must be accompanied by rapid needs assessments and stronger coordination to establish the scale of unmet needs and guide the response. ethiopia.summary: A recent humanitarian assessment highlights the escalating crisis in Ethiopia's Afar, Amhara, and Tigray regions, exacerbated by severe drought, food shortages, and rising child malnutrition rates. The report, dated October 19, reveals that approximately 15% of 11,800 screened children in internally displaced communities in Tigray suffer from moderate acute malnutrition. The ongoing conflict and El Niño-related drought have compounded existing vulnerabilities, leading to significant food insecurity, particularly in southern Tigray, where crop failures have devastated agricultural production. Health services are under severe strain due to insecurity, shortages of medical supplies, and unpaid salaries, causing health workers to leave. Displacement remains a critical issue, with many civilians moving towards Shire amid ongoing hostilities. The assessment emphasizes the urgent need for improved humanitarian access and rapid needs assessments to address the fragmented information and guide responses effectively. Despite some improvements in access, challenges persist, complicating the humanitarian situation further.

ethiopia.title: Liberation Without Domination - Ethiopia's Opposition Alliance and the Right to Decide
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Liberation Without Domination - Ethiopia's Opposition Alliance and the Right to Decide - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Liberation Without Domination - Ethiopia's Opposition Alliance and the Right to Decide 27 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion By Dr. Hambisa Belina Addis Abeba — The Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, or EPFAS, was announced on 20 September 2026. Announced participants included the Oromo Liberation Front-Oromo Liberation Army, known as OLF-OLA, the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). Its statement , reproduced on an OLF-OLA-associated website, proposes an inclusive temporary government, temporary governing rules, and public discussion of the country's political future. The central issue is political authorship: people's continuing power to shape, approve, challenge, and revise the rules and institutions governing their lives. It must operate throughout the struggle and transition. A promised future vote does not, by itself, authorize the powers leaders exercise beforehand. Domination means exposure to power people cannot effectively contest or control, even when no mistreatment occurs and leaders promise to act wisely. Republican political thought calls freedom from this vulnerability non-domination. Applied reciprocally, it protects communities against imposed arrangements and individuals against unchecked authority within them. Neither legal office nor a liberation claim excuses unchecked power. Political authorship makes power answerable at both levels. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Cooperation among former enemies may help stop fighting and enable negotiation. It also raises questions about representation, civilian safety, and governing powers. Incumbents must face the same scrutiny. Existing institutions carry legal responsibilities an opposition statement cannot set aside. Holding office does not excuse ruling through fear; opposing a government does not establish a right to replace it. Different decisions need different permission Three levels of authorization matter. Organizational authorization is a mandate from a movement's members or appropriate internal body, including permission to join an alliance. Alliance authorization concerns participating organizations' rules and limits for cooperation. Constituent authorization comes from the people bound by decisions about their political status or constitutional future. Authority at one level does not automatically confer authority at another. Temporary government also needs separate public authorization and a lawful basis for its powers. Joining an alliance need not require a referendum. Negotiators may arrange a ceasefire without authority to decide borders, appoint a government, or settle whether a people remains in a federation or becomes independent. Each decision needs authority appropriate to its consequences. The available public documents, examined through 14 October 2026, record promises of public choice alongside objections and contested participation. ACLED reported that the Gumuz movement denied joining and that rival Ogaden National Liberation Front factions disputed participation. Published reactions also differ. Advocacy for Oromia rejected EPFAS, arguing that it inadequately addressed Oromo grievances and historical redress. T. M. Asfaw opposed cooperation over divergent political projects and risks to Fano's cohesion; Habte H. urged that EPFAS be judged by civilian protection and the accountability of any transitional government. These positions raise questions for leaders; none measures public opinion. The reviewed documents do not establish specific instructions authorizing representatives to join EPFAS or agreed public procedures for approving temporary appointments and governing powers. Nor do they establish an agreed alliance choice among federation, a negotiated political relationship, and independence for Oromia or other peoples. Undisclosed arrangements cannot simply be presumed absent, but the public needs more than assurances. A promised future vote does not, by itself, authorize the powers leaders exercise beforehand." The statements and interviews reviewed here do not establish what most of the Oromo, Amharas, Tigrayans, or others want. Support for a movement, its alliance, and a particular settlement are separate questions. Leaders must discover those differences and let them affect decisions. Listening must be able to change decisions The Brazilian educator Paulo Freire offers a demanding understanding of liberation. People must take part in understanding their circumstances and shaping the effort to change them. Leaders have to learn from those experiences, explain their own thinking, and revise it through dialogue. Reflection and action belong together: people and leaders act, examine the consequences, and learn how to proceed. Frantz Fanon warned that liberation could replace officeholders while ordinary people remained excluded from governing. Freire offers a response: leaders and communities learn through dialogue, and public criticism must be able to change strategy and the terms of delegated authority. Listening helps a struggle avoid reproducing the domination it opposes. Engagement must begin while choices remain open and continue throughout the struggle. Meetings held only after decisions are settled give people little influence. Leaders should explain which proposals changed because people challenged them and give reasons for rejecting others. A community may be concerned about unsafe roads, missing relatives, or farmland access, while its leaders prioritize an alliance. Engagement must address both sets of concerns. Usable information and independent space to propose alternatives can reveal dangers or priorities leaders have overlooked. The OLF-OLA's 2023 manifesto affirms Oromo self-determination and freely elected representatives. Its members' approval cannot substitute for the choices of everyone it claims to represent. Leaders' interests and public preferences may differ; continuing engagement helps expose and address that difference. The Oromo Liberation Front--Adda Bilisummaa Oromoo (ABO) in Afaan Oromo--reported adopting a political program at its August 2017 congress . The program, according to a nonpublic copy consulted by the author, advocated an independent Oromia while pledging to respect the Oromo people's decision on self-determination and making political association conditional on public choice. It records an organizational position at that time; it does not establish present public preferences or an EPFAS-specific mandate for today's OLF-OLA. Advocating a constitutional outcome does not, by itself, give an organization authority to decide that outcome for the people. In the BBC's Afaan Oromo interview account , adviser Jireenyaa Guddataa describes procedural cooperation rather than a merger, with organizations retaining separate leadership, programs, and forces. He says the public should decide unresolved political questions. These explanations clarify the movement's position; they do not establish agreed alliance rules or public approval. Operational secrecy may protect lives but needs specific reasons, limited scope, and independent review. It cannot justify blanket secrecy about political commitments or postponing accountability until victory. People must be able to criticize strategy without being branded enemies of the struggle. Discussion must reach people outside party structures and those pushed out of public life. Women, young people, displaced families, farmers, pastoralists, workers, and minority residents need safe opportunities to shape what gets discussed. Commanders, donors, officials, and customary leaders should not control who gets heard. Five questions can turn the principles of non-domination and leadership through dialogue into a practical test of political authorship: Who claims to speak on whose behalf? Who has granted them the authority to make decisions, what decisions are they authorized to make, and for how long? Can those affected raise their own priorities and challenge proposals without fear of reprisal? How will each decision be approved through a fair process? Finally, how can people challenge a wrong, replace their representatives, or reclaim powers they have delegated? Freedom for Oromia must protect everyone Reciprocal non-domination requires the Oromo people's real authority over political arrangements and protection against arbitrary power for every individual in Oromia. Equal rights belong to everyone, regardless of ethnicity, gender, religion, political affiliation, or social status. Political authorship gives people continuing control over governing institutions; equal rights limit even publicly authorized leaders. An Oromo-led government can still dominate residents who cannot effectively challenge its decisions. The principle extends across communities. Those demanding freedom from imposed rule must respect other peoples' corresponding freedom. No alliance vote gives one movement authority to decide another people's status or settle a disputed territory by military force. Respect for these rights must not depend on an opponent showing the same restraint. A reformed federation, a new agreed political relationship among peoples, and independence for Oromia or other peoples must remain open to peaceful debate. Ethiopia's Constitution recognizes self-determination, including the right to form an independent state, and sets procedures for exercising it. It also protects equality and political participation. Collective rights and residents' individual rights both matter. Article 39(4) specifies how secession may be exercised: a demand approved by two-thirds of the legislative council of the people concerned, a federally organized referendum within three years of the federal government receiving the council's decision, and, if a majority supports secession, transfer of powers and division of assets as prescribed by law. Border disputes and constitutional amendments have separate procedures. Following these procedures does not, by itself, eliminate coercion or exclusion, but neither an alliance agreement nor military control substitutes for a lawful constituent decision. The Oromo people's collective rights, Oromia's governmental powers, and residents' individual rights are connected but distinct. Rules for selecting delegates or voters must be publicly explained, respect collective rights, protect residents and displaced people, and allow independent challenges. Neither control of a disputed area nor forced displacement may determine whose voice counts. Shared institutions may be needed for security, revenues, transport, and public services. Their powers should be agreed, limited, and open to challenge. This does not give every local leader a veto over ordinary common decisions. Fair procedures can produce binding decisions despite disagreement, while protecting those who lose a vote. Political authorship concerns who may exercise authority and how people hold it answerable. Reciprocal non-domination limits every actor's conduct, authorized or not. Civilian protection is an immediate obligation. Civilian protection cannot wait ACLED reported that an August 2026 ambush by the Bizamo Command in western Oromia killed at least sixteen people, including eleven civilians and five soldiers. It also reported that the Amhara Fano National Movement, later announced as an EPFAS participant, claimed Bizamo fell under its command. How can OLF-OLA justify cooperation with a partner claiming command over a unit implicated in killing civilians in Oromia? Each partner must prevent forces under its control from attacking civilians, including those another partner claims to represent, and support independent investigation and accountability. Scrutiny must also reach OLF-OLA. Amnesty International's 2026 briefing documented ten survivors' accounts of sexual violence in western Oromia, supported by medical evidence. Survivors identified OLF-OLA fighters; one also identified an Ethiopian army soldier. Amnesty could not verify the named individuals' identities. These accounts demand survivor protection and independent investigation, without assigning guilt to an entire organization. OLF-OLA's manifesto calls for independent investigation. In the BBC account, Guddataa disputes allegations against the movement while pledging punishment of offenders under its control. These statements require independent testing; the manifesto's general commitments are not a specific response to Amnesty's later findings. Government authority likewise requires scrutiny. Human Rights Watch's 2026 country report , covering 2025, describes abuses during armed conflict and government repression of independent media and civil society. A 2024 Reuters investigation reported extrajudicial killings and unlawful detention linked to Oromia's Koree Nageenyaa security committee. The same investigation reported that the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission's head confirmed the committee's existence and said it had exceeded its mandate. Liberation without a new dominator means that those acting in the people's name remain within the people's reach." Holding all actors to standards of protection does not mean that every allegation rests on equally strong evidence or that responsibility is equal. Every force must prevent attacks on civilians, sexual violence, forced displacement, child recruitment, and obstruction of relief. Survivors need care, safe reporting, and access to justice. These duties apply immediately, whether or not an actor has public permission to govern. Temporary power needs limits from the start A future vote cannot automatically authorize everything leaders do before it. Temporary administrations may shape constitutional choice by appointing officials, selecting participants, controlling security, or narrowing the options people may debate. Before exercising discretionary power, a temporary administration needs a publicly approved mandate. People must know who selected it, who approved its powers, what it may do, and when its authority expires. Independent civilian oversight and legal review must enable changes to appointments or decisions. Where safe elections are impossible, temporary arrangements need open selection rules, nominations from political, community, and independent civic groups, protected objections, and early public review. Authority must remain limited, and successful challenges must be able to change appointments or mandates. Calling a body inclusive establishes neither representation of everyone nor authority to decide the constitutional future. Who authorizes the body setting these selection rules? Publicly justified procedures involving affected communities' representatives and diverse civic groups must determine its membership and mandates. Minorities, displaced people, and politically unaffiliated residents must have a protected right to participate. Those procedures must also face independent legal review. A civilian body can help legally authorized institutions develop separate procedures for consultation, delegate selection, and referendum eligibility. Calling itself representative confers no authority to make binding rules. Without a full public mandate, provisional authority must remain especially narrow, temporary, and reviewable. Different tasks require different thresholds. Ceasefire talks, relief access, and indispensable services may proceed lawfully under narrow, reviewable powers without a constituent vote. Governing appointments, security, and budgets need time-limited public authorization and lawful authority. Final status and foundational constitutional arrangements require constituent decisions. Urgency creates no general license to govern. Article 9(3) of Ethiopia's Constitution prohibits assuming state power outside constitutional procedures. The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance , ratified by Ethiopia, treats replacement of a democratically elected government by armed dissidents or rebels as unconstitutional; application depends on the government's democratic character and particular facts. Neither victory nor public support alone makes an administration lawful. Lawfully holding public office does not justify coercion or the permanent denial of recognized rights. Where institutions obstruct those rights, negotiated constitutional change requires disclosed negotiating mandates, an account of the obstruction and legal status, and protection of competing choices. Obstruction does not transfer constituent authority to commanders. Peace must reach everyday life Political authorship also matters in decisions about land, livelihoods, resources, and everyday life, beyond governments and constitutions. Oromo political thought helps connect these safeguards to everyday relationships. Safuu holds those in authority accountable to standards of restraint, dignity, and responsibility toward others and the living environment. Gadaa's traditions of deliberation and succession offer lessons about limited office and public assessment of leaders. Women's institutions such as Siiqqee also express capacities to organize and challenge wrongdoing. These traditions vary and have changed over time. Historical gender and status inequalities require critical scrutiny. Contemporary institutions drawing on them must protect equal rights and remain answerable to residents with different beliefs. Nagaa connects peace with just coexistence among people and their surroundings. Applied to a political settlement, it directs attention to whether displaced families can return safely, livelihoods can recover, water is clean, and injuries receive a fair hearing. A ceasefire deserves protection even while that work remains unfinished. Together, Safuu, Gadaa, and Nagaa connect political authorship to ethical restraint, public review of officeholders, and material repair. They deepen Freire's demand for continuing public control: even a government chosen through fair procedures can dominate when decisions affecting land, livelihoods, or the environment remain beyond effective challenge. This tests promises of change: people need meaningful influence over land, mining, development, and public money, with effective ways to challenge harm. The proposed Addis Ababa-Oromia Master Plan raised fears that capital expansion would displace Oromo farmers. Protests met a violent crackdown; the plan was canceled in January 2016. That reversal showed protest could change policy; it did not establish lasting public control over land. Replacing officeholders can leave familiar power intact if land and resource decisions remain beyond public control. EPFAS should be judged by the powers it claims and decisions it makes, with the same scrutiny applied to incumbents and other actors. Political authorship must extend through struggle, temporary government, and final settlement, with people able to authorize decisions, challenge them, and secure change through fair procedures. Liberation without a new dominator means that those acting in the people's name remain within the people's reach. AS Editor's Note : Dr. Hambisa Belina is an associate professor of accounting
ethiopia.summary: The Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival (EPFAS), formed on September 20, 2026, includes the Oromo Liberation Front-Oromo Liberation Army (OLF-OLA), the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). The alliance advocates for an inclusive temporary government and emphasizes the importance of political authorship, where the people retain the power to shape their governance. The article critiques the potential for domination within this alliance, arguing that authority must be derived from the people and that leaders should be accountable to their constituents. It highlights the need for ongoing public engagement and dialogue to ensure that diverse voices, including marginalized groups, are heard in decision-making processes. The article also stresses that any political arrangements must respect the rights of all ethnic groups and individuals, advocating for a lawful approach to self-determination and governance in Ethiopia. Ultimately, it calls for a political environment where power is answerable and non-domination is prioritized.

ethiopia.title: More Than 60 Killed in Oromia as Ethiopia’s Instability Deepens, Raising Alarm for Mogadishu - FTL Somalia
ethiopia.content: More Than 60 Killed in Oromia as Ethiopia's Instability Deepens, Raising Alarm for Mogadishu - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Security Nationwide More Than 60 Killed in Oromia as Ethiopia’s Instability Deepens, Raising Alarm for Mogadishu October 27, 2026 6 min read MOGADISHU , The massacre of more than 60 Christians in Ethiopia’s Oromia region is not a distant tragedy for Somalia. It is a direct indicator of the escalating instability in a neighboring state whose internal conflicts are increasingly intertwined with Somalia’s own security and political trajectory. A Pattern of Sectarian Violence According to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, more than 60 people were killed in attacks on three areas in the Shirka district of Oromia. A local official blamed the Alliance for Survival, a newly formed rebel coalition that includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has denied involvement in previous such attacks. Eyewitnesses told BBC Amharic that five of those killed were children, and that 20 houses were burned to the ground. The Ethiopian Human Rights Council reported in July 2026 that 458 people had been killed in attacks in that area over the previous four years, describing them as religiously motivated and targeting followers of the Orthodox Church. This latest massacre is one of the deadliest in that period. The Rebel Alliance Behind the Chaos The Shirka killings are part of a wider pattern of escalating violence across Ethiopia. A coalition of seven armed groups, including the TPLF, the Fano militia in Amhara, and the OLA, has announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the alliance , the coalition spans half of Ethiopia’s twelve regional states and brings together groups that have previously fought one another, making the alignment an unusual development in the country’s fragmented opposition landscape. The Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), a Somali-majority armed group, is among the signatories. Its inclusion is particularly notable given the group’s 2018 peace agreement with the Ethiopian government and its subsequent focus on diplomatic efforts to advance the interests of ethnic Somalis in Ethiopia’s Somali Regional State. The Moyale Clashes: A Somali Dimension The violence in Oromia directly affects ethnic Somali communities in Ethiopia. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Moyale clashes , heavy fighting erupted between Oromo and Somali communities in the border town, killing at least nine people and forcing more than 2,500 Ethiopians to flee into Kenya. The trigger was a dispute over the display of the Somali Regional State flag at an administrative office in an area administered by Oromia. These clashes demonstrate how local disputes over flags, administrative boundaries, and political control can escalate into deadly confrontations with regional consequences. For Somalia, the displacement of ethnic Somalis across the border into Kenya carries humanitarian and security implications, particularly in a borderland region where Al-Shabaab has historically exploited instability. What This Means for Somalia: The Security Gap For Somalia, the implications are direct and urgent. Ethiopia’s internal conflicts are already drawing its military resources away from Somalia. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Ethiopia’s military redeployment , Addis Ababa is planning to withdraw more than 3,000 troops from the Bay and Bakool regions of South West State to redeploy them to Tigray, Amhara, and Afar. This withdrawal would leave a security gap in areas where Ethiopian forces have been fighting Al-Shabaab, and it comes as the AUSSOM mission faces its own funding and mandate uncertainties. The timing is particularly delicate. The UN political mission in Somalia is closing its doors on October 31, ending more than three decades of international political stewardship. The AUSSOM mission faces a funding cliff and a potential withdrawal of Ugandan forces. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the transition , Somalia is entering a phase where it will have fewer international buffers and more direct responsibility for its own security. Ethiopia’s regional position is also hardening. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Ethiopia’s response to the Alamein Declaration , Addis Ababa has rejected what it describes as “coercive measures” and “acts of destabilization” aimed at constraining its Red Sea ambitions. The four-nation Alamein Declaration, signed by Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia, and Sudan, formalized coordination on regional security and affirmed that Red Sea governance is the responsibility of littoral states. Ethiopia’s exclusion from that framework, combined with its internal conflicts, creates a volatile regional dynamic. Critical Note The massacre in Shirka is a crime that demands accountability, and the Ethiopian government’s failure to protect its citizens, particularly religious minorities, is a damning indictment of its security apparatus. The Orthodox Church’s statement that it had repeatedly raised concerns with authorities but received no solution is a familiar refrain in Ethiopia, where local communities have borne the brunt of conflicts that the state is either unable or unwilling to contain. For Somalia, the lesson is one of exposure. Ethiopia’s internal fragmentation is not a spectator sport. It is a process that is already reshaping the security architecture of the Horn of Africa. The withdrawal of Ethiopian troops from Somalia, the displacement of civilians across the Kenyan border, and the formation of a rebel alliance that includes armed groups from multiple regions all point in the same direction: Ethiopia is entering a period of prolonged instability, and Somalia will feel the consequences whether it is prepared or not. The Somali government’s focus on its own political crisis, the contested electoral process, and the fight against Al-Shabaab is understandable. But it cannot afford to ignore the collapse of order next door. The same international partners who are withdrawing from Somalia are also watching Ethiopia with concern. The same Al-Shabaab that Somalia is fighting has exploited Ethiopian instability in the past. The same borderlands that are now scenes of sectarian violence are the corridors through which weapons, fighters, and displaced people move. The Shirka massacre is a warning. It is not the first, and it will not be the last. Somalia’s security is not confined to its borders. It is shaped by the stability of its neighbors, and Ethiopia’s stability is deteriorating rapidly. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church reported that the victims were targeted in attacks attributed to a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). ethiopia.content: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 27, 2026 - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: All of Africa Today - October 27, 2026 AllAfrica AllAfrica logo 27 October 2026 allAfrica.com By Melody Chironda More Than 60 Killed In Attacks In Ethiopia More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks targeting Christian communities in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The attacks occurred in three areas of the Shirka district, where at least 20 houses were reportedly burnt down, and five children were among those killed. One resident described the violence as an ambush, saying attackers surrounded the community from all sides. A church official called the incident a massacre, adding that security forces arrived but were unable to stop the assault. Many residents have since fled the area. A local official blamed a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has not commented on the latest allegations and previously denied responsibility for similar attacks. The Orthodox Church condemned the violence, saying attacks against Christians have increased and accusing authorities of failing to address repeated concerns about insecurity. A July 2026 report by the Ethiopian Human Rights Council recorded 458 deaths in attacks in the area over the previous four years, identifying local communities, particularly Orthodox Christians, as frequent targets. However, previous reports have also documented attacks against Muslims, with residents describing the violence as both ethnic and religious in nature. Algeria Approves Troop Deployment To Niger Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Algeria is preparing to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger in its first foreign military deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war. The proposed deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister as the country seeks assistance in combating armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State. Algeria's parliament approved the deployment, with 148 of 174 senators voting in favour before the lower house also backed the move. Algeria has not yet announced the timing or number of troops, but they are expected to help secure energy infrastructure in northern Niger, near the Libyan border. The operation would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision permitting overseas military deployments and a significant departure from Algeria's longstanding opposition to sending troops abroad. Algerian officials have stressed that the mission is intended to protect economic infrastructure rather than wage war. The country has significant economic interests in Niger, including a proposed gas pipeline that would transport Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria. UN Warns 3.6 Million in Uganda Facing Acute Food Insecurity as Crisis Worsens About 3.6 million people in Uganda face high levels of acute food insecurity, and the number is projected to rise to 4.4 million between February and June 2027, according to the 2026 Integrated Food Security Phase Classification report. Refugees and communities in the Karamoja sub-region are expected to face the greatest burden as food shortages and malnutrition worsen. The report estimates that 465,900 children under five and 246,300 pregnant and breastfeeding women will require treatment for acute malnutrition between April 2026 and March 2027. The crisis is being driven by recurring climate shocks, declining agricultural production, crop and livestock pests and diseases, high food prices, deteriorating livelihoods and limited access to healthcare, clean water, sanitation and social protection. United Nations Resident Coordinator in Uganda Leonard Zulu called for urgent action to protect vulnerable households and strengthen food systems before conditions deteriorate further. Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja urged the government, development partners and humanitarian agencies to invest in sustainable solutions that enable communities to produce their own food and reduce dependence on emergency assistance. The assessment, conducted across 60 districts between August and September 2026, was launched alongside a $50 million joint appeal by the United Nations and its partners to support emergency responses in Karamoja and early interventions in 37 districts and eight refugee settlements. The proposed response includes cash assistance, agricultural and livestock support, nutrition screening and treatment, healthcare, child protection, gender-based violence prevention, water and sanitation programmes, and disaster preparedness. The report warns that without sustained investment and coordinated action, vulnerable communities could face worsening hunger and malnutrition in the coming months. Amnesty Warns Funding Crisis Could Shut Central African Republic War Crimes Court Amnesty International has warned that suspected perpetrators of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Central African Republic (CAR), including senior officials, could escape justice if the country's Special Criminal Court (SCC) fails to secure urgent funding. In a report released in October 2026, the organisation said the court, inaugurated in 2018, has tried six cases and secured convictions against 19 people for war crimes and crimes against humanity, with reparations awarded to victims in one case. However, many survivors of atrocities committed during the 2003 coup and the 2012–2014 armed conflict are still waiting for those responsible to be prosecuted. The United States withdrew its funding in 2025, leaving more than US$4.15 million in unpaid commitments and plunging the court into an unprecedented financial crisis. The United Nations and European Union are now its only financial contributors, while funding shortages have forced staff reductions, including cuts to the witness protection unit, and prevented prosecutors from opening new investigations. Amnesty warned that the court could close when its mandate expires in October 2028 unless additional funding is secured. Ukraine Allegedly Supporting Mali Militia Ukraine is facing questions over its alleged involvement in supporting Tuareg fighters in northern Mali, a development that could extend its rivalry with Russia into Africa's Sahel region. A September 2026 CNN investigation reported that around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists were assisting Tuareg fighters, although DW said it had not independently verified the claims and Ukraine has not confirmed a specific operation. Analysts believe any involvement would fit Kyiv's broader strategy of weakening Russian influence internationally, particularly in countries where Moscow provides military support to governments. Mali's military authorities have increasingly relied on Russia for security assistance since taking power in coups in 2020 and 2021, with Russia's Africa Corps replacing the Wagner Group's role in 2025. Local officials attributed the assaults to a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Delivers Over 1 Million Digital Business Registration, Licensing Services
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Delivers Over 1 Million Digital Business Registration, Licensing Services - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Delivers Over 1 Million Digital Business Registration, Licensing Services 26 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia provided more than 1.08 million business registration and licensing services digitally over a three-month period, according to the Ministry of Trade and Regional Integration. The milestone highlights ongoing national efforts to streamline business procedures and expand online public services. The ministry's latest online services report reveals that 1,088,787 services were delivered across federal institutions, regional states, and city administrations, underscoring the expanding role of digital platforms in the country's commercial administration. Among the regions, Oromia Regional State recorded the highest volume with 441,550 services provided. Addis Ababa followed with 204,512, Amhara with 156,193, and South Ethiopia with 101,891. By service category, trade name clearance accounted for the largest share, with 579,785 services delivered. Business license renewals followed with 122,730, while license amendments totaled 107,317. New business registrations accounted for 60,409 services. The ministry said the digital system was helping reduce bureaucratic burdens on the business community while improving the efficiency, accessibility and transparency of public service delivery. The expansion of digital business registration and licensing services is part of Ethiopia's broader digital transformation agenda, which aims to modernize public administration, simplify procedures and improve access to government services through technology. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia has successfully delivered over 1.08 million digital business registration and licensing services within a three-month period, as reported by the Ministry of Trade and Regional Integration. This achievement reflects the country's commitment to enhancing business procedures and expanding online public services. The report indicates that 1,088,787 services were provided across various federal institutions, regional states, and city administrations, with Oromia Regional State leading at 441,550 services. Addis Ababa and Amhara followed with 204,512 and 156,193 services, respectively. The most common service was trade name clearance, accounting for 579,785 services, while business license renewals and amendments also contributed significantly. The digital system aims to alleviate bureaucratic challenges for businesses, improving efficiency, accessibility, and transparency in public service delivery. This initiative is part of Ethiopia's broader digital transformation agenda, which seeks to modernize public administration and enhance access to government services through technology.

ethiopia.title: ICRC Reaffirms Commitment to Partnership With Ethiopia
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: ICRC Reaffirms Commitment to Partnership With Ethiopia - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: ICRC Reaffirms Commitment to Partnership With Ethiopia 26 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening its partnership with Ethiopia, commending the humanitarian efforts of the Ethiopian Red Cross Society (ERCS). During discussions with President Taye Atske Selassie, ICRC Regional Director for Africa Mamadou Sow praised the ERCS for its humanitarian work across the country and emphasized the importance of international humanitarian law and strong leadership in ensuring that essential assistance reaches people in need. President Taye and Mamadou Sow discussed the validity and the importance of international humanitarian law. Sow also commended President Taye for promoting cooperation among key Ethiopian government institutions, including the Ministries of Health, Justice and Defense. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He expressed appreciation for the access and acceptance granted to the ICRC in Ethiopia, which enable the organization to carry out its humanitarian operations. Highlighting the importance of collaboration with the ERCS, Sow described the organization as a key partner in implementing programs focused on water, health and food security across Ethiopia. "The Ethiopian Red Cross is a marvelous organization," Sow said. "It's our privileged partner in this country, with whom we work across Ethiopia on water, health, and food security." He also praised the ERCS's extensive volunteer network, describing volunteers as the backbone of the organization and the wider International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement. "We are very proud of that partnership because it relies on so many volunteers who are the beating heart of our global movement," Sow added. "We take great pride in their work, as well as the strong support Ethiopia provides to its Red Cross society." Read the original article on ENA . somalia.content: UN mission in Somalia to end operations on Oct. 31 after decades of support - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY UN mission in Somalia to end operations on Oct. 31 after decades of support Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Diyar Guldogan Tuesday October 27, 2026 'This milestone brings to a close more than three decades of United Nations missions in support of peacebuilding, state-building, governance and reconciliation in Somalia,’ says spokesman The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will conclude its mandate on Oct. 31, ending a two-year transition and more than three decades of UN missions supporting peacebuilding, governance and state-building in the country, a UN official said Monday. In a statement, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ spokesman, Stephane Dujarric, said the mission would cease operations in accordance with Security Council resolutions and a request from Somalia’s federal government. advertisements “This milestone brings to a close more than three decades of United Nations missions in support of peacebuilding, state-building, governance and reconciliation in Somalia,” Dujarric said. The closure follows a jointly agreed transition roadmap under which UNTMIS’s mandated responsibilities have been transferred to Somali institutions and UN agencies, funds and programmes. Guterres reaffirmed that the UN would continue supporting Somalia through its resident agencies and programmes, working with Somali authorities, the African Union and other international partners to promote peace, stability, human rights and sustainable development, Dujarric said. “Recognizing the significant political, security, humanitarian and development challenges that remain, the Secretary-General calls for sustained international support to consolidate progress, advance inclusive political dialogue and reconciliation, strengthen institutions, and promote and protect human rights,” he added. Dujarric stressed that Guterres reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to the people of Somalia and to supporting Somali-led efforts to build a peaceful, stable and prosperous future. somalia.summary: The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will conclude its operations on October 31, marking the end of over three decades of UN involvement in the country. This decision follows a two-year transition period and aligns with requests from Somalia's federal government and Security Council resolutions. UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric emphasized that this milestone signifies the transfer of UNTMIS responsibilities to Somali institutions and various UN agencies. Despite the mission's closure, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres assured continued support for Somalia through resident agencies, focusing on peace, stability, human rights, and sustainable development. He highlighted the ongoing political, security, and humanitarian challenges in the country, calling for sustained international support to foster political dialogue, reconciliation, and institutional strengthening. Guterres reaffirmed the UN's commitment to aiding Somalia in its efforts to achieve a peaceful and prosperous future.

somalia.title: Somalia opens fourth national cybersecurity forum as digital security efforts expand - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia opens fourth national cybersecurity forum as digital security efforts expand - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia opens fourth national cybersecurity forum as digital security efforts expand Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday October 27, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali federal government opened its fourth National Cyber Security Forum on Tuesday in Mogadishu as the country expands efforts to protect its growing digital infrastructure. The two-day forum, organized by the National Communications Authority (NCA) and Mogadishu University, is being held under the theme “Building Trust and Cyber Resilience Through Security by Design.” advertisements The forum focuses on cybersecurity governance, protecting digital infrastructure, addressing emerging threats and strengthening national incident response capabilities. It also emphasizes integrating security measures into digital systems from the outset rather than introducing them after deployment. “Cybersecurity is a shared responsibility that requires collaboration among government, academia, private sector, and society,” Mogadishu University President Ibrahim Mohamed Mursal said. “Universities have an important role in developing the skills and research needed to address emerging cybersecurity issues.” Mursal also highlighted the university’s establishment of a new Department of Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence. Mr. Mustafa Yasin Sheikh, Director General of the NCA, highlighted key cybersecurity achievements, including the launch of the Somali Computer Incident Response Team (SOMCIRT), capacity-building programs for government officials, public awareness initiatives, and the development of cybersecurity risk and compliance management frameworks. “The progress we have made this year provides an important foundation for strengthening cybersecurity in Somalia. This forum offers an opportunity to share knowledge, research and expertise, and develop practical solutions to advance our national cybersecurity efforts,” he said. SOMCIRT was inaugurated on March 7 as Somalia’s first national center dedicated to coordinating the prevention, detection and response to cyber incidents. It operates under the communications authority and is responsible for receiving incident reports, issuing alerts and coordinating responses to threats affecting government institutions and critical infrastructure. The communications authority also completed its first cybersecurity certification program for government officials this year, training information technology professionals from 21 public institutions in internationally recognized cybersecurity standards and practices. Communications and Technology Minister Mohamed Adan Mo’allin who officially opened Tuesday’s forum said the government also plans to establish a National Cybersecurity Academy. “I hope this forum will produce practical outcomes that benefit the Somali people,” he said. Somalia has accelerated efforts to build a national cybersecurity framework as government services, telecommunications, banking and other sectors increasingly rely on digital systems. The House of the People approved a cybersecurity law in January establishing responsibilities for government agencies, critical infrastructure operators and national incident reporting and response. The law also formally provides for SOMCIRT. The National Cyber Security Forum was first held in Mogadishu in 2023. Previous editions have brought together public and private-sector institutions to discuss cyber threats, policy development, information sharing and protection of critical infrastructure. Topics Charities About Our Office News & Information File a Complaint Order Publications Contact Us Search Our Site Attorney General Ellison again leads court defense of Temporary Protected Status for immigrants from Somalia Leads coalition of 17 AGs in amicus brief asking federal court to hear appeal; second time this year AG Ellison and coalition have supported TPS for Somali Americans October 27, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — For the second time this year, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has led a coalition of 17 attorneys general in filing an amicus brief in support of a lawsuit to block Department of Homeland Security’s termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Somali immigrants . The TPS program is a crucial humanitarian lifeline that Congress established in the 1990 to protect immigrants from being returned to countries like Somalia that have been deemed unsafe, allowing them to work and build a life in the United States. Approximately 3,850 immigrants from Somalia have been living in the United States with TPS or have had pending applications for TPS, many of them in Minnesota. “The Trump Administration’s insistence on terminating Temporary Protected Status for Somali nationals isn’t only cruel, it’s harmful to communities across Minnesota and in every state where Somalis live, work, grow the economy, pay taxes, and give back,” Attorney General Ellison said. “I led this coalition of attorneys general supporting the plaintiffs who want to block the revocation of TPS for Somalis because we recognize the contributions of our Somali neighbors that strengthen our states and our people and do not want our states to be harmed if the revocation is allowed to stand.” This is the second amicus brief that Attorney General Ellison led this year of attorneys general defending Somali TPS , following the first one he led in April 2026 . The brief filed yesterday in African Communities Together v. Mullin supports the plaintiffs’ request that the appeals court reverse a lower court decision not to grant emergency relief and block the Department of Homeland Security’s revocation of TPS for Somali nationals. The coalition states are home to at least 53,000 Somali immigrants, with Minnesota alone home to at least 37,500. These numbers include TPS holders, whom the coalition states have taken public steps to support because Somali immigrants, including TPS holders, make vital contributions to the communities in which they live: they are valued neighbors, homeowners, coworkers, teachers, students, entrepreneurs, caregivers, construction workers, union members, and parents. Stripping TPS holders of legal status would harm the residents, economies, and public health and safety of Minnesota and the coalition states. In the brief , Attorney General Ellison and the coalition highlight the harms Minnesota and the coalition states and their residents — including the U.S. citizen children of Somali nationals with TPS — will experience with the revocation of TPS for Somalis, arguing that it would harm their states’ economies, residents, and public health and safety. Somali immigrants make a significant, positive impact on Minnesota’s economy: their annual economic impact is roughly $8.6 billion and they pay an estimated $228 million annually in state and local taxes. They also contribute to critical industries: as of 2019, over 15 percent of all Somali immigrants in Minnesota worked in home health care, and Somali workers made up 11 percent of the state’s workers in animal food processing. Somali immigrants are also known for their entrepreneurship, starting businesses that create jobs, circulate dollars locally, and revitalize communities. The Minnesota Department of Economic Development has recognized that “[w]ithout foreign-born workers,” of which Somalis are the second-largest group in Minnesota, “many businesses in Minnesota would not have the workers they need to operate, let alone grow and thrive.” Allowing the revocation of Somalia’s TPS designation to stand endangers these economic contributions to communities in every corner of Minnesota. Creating new undocumented citizens by revoking TPS for Somali nationals would have ripple effects throughout educational and public-health systems. Operation Metro Surge, the purpose of which President Trump claimed was to root out fraud in Somali communities in Minnesota, led to high rates of absenteeism throughout public schools in Minneapolis, including of U.S. citizen children of Somali immigrants — many of whom themselves are U.S. citizens. Stripping legal status from Somali immigrants also risks serious negative consequences for public health. Everyone benefits when residents are vaccinated or seek testing and treatment for infectious diseases. But undocumented immigrants are often reluctant to seek medical treatment due to fear of detention and deportation. Newly undocumented former TPS holders may also not seek treatment for their U.S. citizen children. Children of undocumented immigrants frequently miss preventive annual exams and are often sicker when seeking emergency room care. In Minneapolis, 40 percent of respondents to a recent survey who needed to go to urgent care or the hospital during Operation Metro Surge reported they stayed home because of fears about ICE agents, and 30 percent of respondents who had a regularly scheduled vaccine during the operation missed the vaccine out of the same fears. The impacts on the mental health and well-being of revoking TPS for Somali nationals on their U.S. citizen children would also be severe. Children of undocumented parents in the United States frequently experience persistent anxiety from fear that a family member may be deported. During Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota, immigration officers targeted individuals they believed appeared to be Somali regardless of citizenship or immigration status, demonstrating that these fears were unfortunately well founded. Mental health consequences are even more severe when these fears are realized and families are forcibly separated. Parental deportation is deeply traumatic for children and is linked to extreme psychological distress, anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, externalizing behaviors such as aggression, and difficulties sleeping. In the brief, Attorney General Ellison and the coalition note that revoking Somalia’s TPS designation would present current TPS holders, particularly those with U.S. citizen children, with an agonizing choice: return to Somalia alone, leaving their children behind; taking their U.S. citizen children with them to a dangerous country that the children do not know; or staying in the United States without authorization and living with significant fear and uncertainty, knowing they cannot work legally and could be forcibly removed to Somalia at any time. History of TPS for Somali nationals Somalia was first designated for TPS in 1991 by Acting Attorney General William Barr due to “extraordinary and temporary conditions.” Civil war has raged in Somalia for the ensuing 35 years, resulting in hundreds of thousands of deaths, children being forced into combat, extrajudicial killings, sexual and gender-based violence, and other human-rights abuses. Given the ongoing violence and suffering, Somalia’s TPS designation had been continually in place until now. In November 2025, President Trump posted on social media that he was “hereby terminating, effective immediately, the Temporary Protected Status (TPS Program) for Somalis in Minnesota...” Since then, President Trump has repeatedly launched racist attacks against Somali immigrants, calling them “garbage” and “stupid people” with “low IQs” “from a crooked country, disgusting country, one of the worst countries in the world.” In January 2026, Kristi then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem announced she was terminating Somalia’s TPS designation in part even though she did not claim that Somalia as a whole is safe and despite the fact that the U.S. State Department has issued its highest travel advisory for Somalia , warning travelers, “Do not travel to Somalia for any reason,” because of “unrest, crime, kidnapping, terrorism,” and more. Following a June 2026 decision of the U.S. Supreme Court, DHS revoked TPS for immigrants from Somalia on August 14, 2026. Attorney General Ellison led the coalition that filed the amicus brief . Joining Attorney General Ellison in the coalition are the attorneys general of California, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Vermont, and Washington. somalia.summary: Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has once again led a coalition of 17 attorneys general in filing an amicus brief to support the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Somali immigrants, following a lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) decision to terminate TPS. This program, established in the 1990s, protects immigrants from unsafe countries, allowing them to live and work in the U.S. Approximately 3,850 Somali immigrants are currently under TPS, with many residing in Minnesota. Ellison argues that ending TPS would harm communities and economies, as Somali immigrants contribute significantly to Minnesota's workforce and economy, generating an estimated $8.6 billion annually. The brief emphasizes the negative impacts on public health and education, particularly for U.S. citizen children of TPS holders, who may face anxiety and trauma from potential family separation. This is the second amicus brief filed by Ellison this year, highlighting ongoing concerns about the welfare of Somali immigrants in the U.S.

somalia.title: Somalia Army Losses Mount After Deadly Militant Attack - kulu-media.com
somalia.content: Somalia Army Losses Mount After Deadly Militant Attack | Kulu Media Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Connect with us Search Kulu Media Somali Troops Report Heavy Casualties in Al-Shabaab Battle Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Home » News » Africa » Horn of Africa » Somali Troops Report Heavy Casualties in Al-Shabaab Battle Horn of Africa Somali Troops Report Heavy Casualties in Al-Shabaab Battle Published 47 minutes ago on October 27, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Somali National Army Gorgor troops patrol a rural area in Somalia. File photo. Photo Credit: SONNA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Dozens of Somali soldiers were reportedly killed and more than 100 wounded during intense fighting with Al-Shabaab militants in southern Somalia, according to military personnel interviewed by Reuters, raising questions about the scale of government losses in a major counterinsurgency operation. The fighting took place on October 26, 2026, in the Jameeco area of Buurhakaba district in Somalia’s Bay region, where government troops were conducting an offensive against Al-Shabaab positions. The Reuters investigation , published on October 27, included accounts from two Somali soldiers who described substantial casualties among government forces. One soldier, identified as Ahmed, said he helped transport 40 dead soldiers and more than 100 wounded personnel to hospitals in Mogadishu following the battle. Another soldier, identified as Farah, said Al-Shabaab fighters had used explosives-laden vehicles against government positions, destroying five military vehicles and killing dozens of soldiers. The reported Somali soldiers killed in the fighting have not been independently confirmed, and the government has not released an official casualty figure for its own forces. Somali Government Claims 75 Al-Shabaab Fighters Killed Somalia’s Defence Ministry acknowledged the fighting but provided a different account focused on casualties among Al-Shabaab militants. According to the ministry, approximately 75 militants were killed and another 56 wounded during several hours of combat around Jameeco. The ministry said Al-Shabaab fighters attacked Somali National Army positions using vehicles packed with explosives, damaging military equipment. However, the official statement did not disclose how many government soldiers were killed or wounded. The ministry’s casualty figures for Al-Shabaab have also not been independently verified. The battle occurred during Operation Banooda, a military campaign targeting Al-Shabaab positions along a strategic corridor in southern Somalia. According to Hiiraan Online , government forces had been advancing along the route connecting Baledogle, Leego and Buurhakaba when the fighting intensified. The Defence Ministry said the operation would continue despite the confrontation. Al-Shabaab also claimed to have inflicted heavy casualties on government troops, but its figures have not been independently verified. Strategic Fighting Near Buurhakaba The confrontation occurred near one of southern Somalia’s most important transportation routes. Buurhakaba lies along the main road connecting Mogadishu and Baidoa, a corridor used for commercial transportation, humanitarian deliveries and military movements. Control of this route is important to the federal government’s ability to reinforce its positions in South West State. The surrounding area has experienced growing instability as federal forces confront Al-Shabaab while also facing a separate political and military dispute involving supporters of former South West State President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen. Earlier this month, Laftagareen-aligned fighters seized Buurhakaba and several other towns in the Bay region, prompting preparations for a federal government-backed counteroffensive. Those developments increased pressure on Baidoa, the administrative center of South West State. However, the latest battle near Jameeco involved Al-Shabaab militants and should be distinguished from the separate confrontation between federal troops and Laftagareen-aligned forces. The federal government has previously accused Laftagareen’s supporters of cooperating with Al-Shabaab, allegations they have denied. No independently verified evidence establishes that the two groups coordinated the October 26 battle. Battle Follows Separate Clashes Near Baidoa The reported heavy military losses come amid a broader deterioration in security across parts of southern Somalia. On October 26, federal troops also clashed near Baidoa with fighters loyal to Laftagareen. That confrontation occurred near Burjeedka, on the outskirts of the regional capital, where opposing commanders reported military casualties and made conflicting claims about battlefield control. The two confrontations involved different opposing forces, but both illustrate the complex security environment confronting Somalia’s federal government. The situation has become increasingly difficult as government forces attempt to conduct counterinsurgency operations while responding to armed challenges linked to regional political disputes. Earlier fighting in September also demonstrated the risks associated with the political confrontation, when armed clashes in Baidoa left civilians and combatants injured. The continuing instability threatens transportation routes and communities already affected by conflict and displacement. Al-Shabaab Remains a Major Security Threat Al-Shabaab, an Al-Qaeda-linked armed group, has waged an insurgency against Somalia’s internationally recognized government for nearly two decades. Despite repeated offensives by Somali forces and international partners, the group continues to operate across parts of southern and central Somalia. Its fighters frequently use roadside bombs, suicide attacks and explosives-laden vehicles against military installations, convoys and government facilities. The October 26 battle demonstrates the continuing threat posed by the group’s ability to attack government forces during offensive operations. The reported destruction of military vehicles and the large number of casualties described by soldiers interviewed by Reuters suggest that the confrontation may have imposed substantial operational costs on the Somali National Army. However, the precise extent of those losses remains uncertain. Independent confirmation is also needed to establish whether the fighting resulted in any significant territorial changes. Questions Remain Over Casualties and Military Losses The conflicting accounts have raised questions about the true scale of the battle. Reuters’ interviews provide firsthand testimony concerning government casualties, while Somalia’s Defence Ministry has concentrated on reported militant losses. Neither account has been independently verified in full. The ministry has not publicly confirmed the reported deaths of 40 soldiers or the transportation of more than 100 wounded personnel to Mogadishu. There has also been no independently established assessment of the number of Al-Shabaab fighters killed. The fighting highlights the continuing challenges facing Somalia’s military as it attempts to weaken the insurgency and maintain control of strategically important territory. For now, the confirmed development is that a major confrontation occurred near Jameeco on October 26, with government forces acknowledging the use of explosives-laden vehicles and soldiers subsequently reporting substantial military casualties. The full death toll, extent of equipment losses and battlefield outcome remain subject to further verification.
